lesson.title: Calhoun's Gambit: South Carolina Defies the Union
lesson.summary: When South Carolina declared federal tariffs void within its borders in 1832, Jackson threatened military force to preserve federal authority, and Henry Clay again brokered the compromise that defused the crisis.
lesson.body:
The Nullification Crisis of 1832 and 1833 was a confrontation between the federal government and South Carolina over whether a state could declare a federal law void within its own borders. It became the most serious test of federal authority between the ratification of the Constitution and the Civil War, and it forced President Andrew Jackson to defend the Union against a doctrine championed by his own vice president.

The immediate cause was a series of protective tariffs, especially the Tariff of 1828, which Southerners bitterly nicknamed the Tariff of Abominations, and a follow up tariff in 1832. These tariffs protected Northern manufacturers but raised prices on imported goods that Southern planters relied on, while doing little to help an agricultural economy built around exporting cotton. John C. Calhoun of South Carolina, serving as Jackson's vice president, anonymously authored the South Carolina Exposition and Protest in 1828, laying out a theory that a state could nullify a federal law it judged unconstitutional. Calhoun drew on ideas from the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions of 1798, written by James Madison and Thomas Jefferson to oppose the Alien and Sedition Acts, which had argued that the states, as parties to the constitutional compact, retained the power to judge federal overreach. Nullification pushed that compact theory of federalism much further than Madison or Jefferson had intended.

In November 1832, a South Carolina convention passed an Ordinance of Nullification declaring the 1828 and 1832 tariffs void within the state and threatening secession if the federal government tried to force collection. Jackson, despite his own sympathy for limited federal power on some issues, responded with unmistakable force. In his Proclamation to the People of South Carolina in December 1832, he called nullification an impractical absurdity and a step toward disunion that he would not tolerate, and he asked Congress for authority to use the military to enforce federal law if necessary, which it granted in the Force Bill of 1833.

War was avoided through another compromise engineered by Henry Clay, who worked with Calhoun, now back in the Senate after resigning the vice presidency, to pass the Compromise Tariff of 1833, which gradually lowered tariff rates over the following decade. South Carolina accepted the new tariff and repealed its nullification ordinance, but in a final defiant gesture it also formally nullified the Force Bill, a symbolic act since the law was no longer needed.

The crisis exposed the unresolved tension at the heart of American federalism between national authority and states rights, a tension the Constitution's framers had never fully settled. It also foreshadowed the arguments Southern states would make three decades later when they seceded from the Union, since nullification and secession both rested on the claim that states retained ultimate sovereignty over the federal compact. Jackson's forceful stand preserved federal authority in the short term, but the underlying sectional conflict over tariffs, and increasingly over slavery, would only deepen in the years that followed.
